label: GPT-6.1 Sol
output:
**4 out of 5 stars — a worthwhile improvement, with a few things to know**

We paid $2,140 for the Lindqvist Optics PT-20 from Chancel AV in February 2026, plus $95 for the wall mount. For our congregation, that was a substantial purchase. We had been livestreaming worship with a webcam since 2020, and I wanted more than a slightly nicer version of the same picture. After using the PT-20 for several months, I would buy it again, though I would not tell every small church it needs one.

Our nave is 92 feet long, and the camera is mounted on the balcony rail at the back. The 20x optical zoom lets us get useful views of the pulpit, altar and other parts of the chancel from that distance. It offers 1080p60 video, NDI HX and a plain HDMI output. Power over Ethernet means we only needed one cable up to the balcony, which was a real advantage in our building.

We run it into OBS on our old office PC and stream to YouTube. Most Sundays we have 30–60 viewers. We have nine presets stored: altar, pulpit, lectern, font, choir loft, piano, a wide view and two views of the chancel steps. That has made it practical to follow the service without asking someone to operate a camera continuously. Erik, our 16-year-old acolyte, learned to run it from the free web app on a tablet in one afternoon.

It was not entirely smooth at the beginning. On our first Sunday, the presets had drifted a few degrees by the sermon. A pulpit preset is not much use if it gradually stops pointing at the pulpit. The March firmware update, version 2.4, fixed that for us. I would recommend checking the firmware before your first service rather than discovering the problem during worship.

Autofocus is another limitation. When someone walks between the camera and the pulpit, it can hunt for focus. We now lock the focus on our presets. That works for us, but it was something we had to learn. The manual is thin and badly translated, and I did not find it especially helpful. Marcy at Chancel AV, on the other hand, was excellent on the phone.

The picture is a clear improvement over our old webcam. At the Easter Vigil in April, during the first “Christ the Lord Is Risen Today” with only candles lighting the church, it became grainy but remained usable. The old webcam would have shown little more than dots of light. This is not a claim that the PT-20 produces a beautiful picture in near darkness. It does not. But people at home could still see something of the service.

The most meaningful assessment came from Delores, who is 82 and homebound. She called to say she could finally read the hymn numbers on the board. That matters more to me than most of the specifications.

One important caution: this camera did nothing for our sound problem. Audio is a separate matter, and churches should not spend their whole livestream budget on a camera expecting it to fix everything.

My rating is **4 out of 5 stars**. It has made our livestream more useful to the people who depend on it, and we would buy it again. Still, a congregation under 100 might do perfectly well with something cheaper. Consider your room, your volunteers and what your viewers actually need before spending this much.
